title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: DTE's queue hits 8GW with Oracle and Google deals—what it means for bills and local resources.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. Today we're diving into the biggest power demand spike yet from these projects.
That's right—DTE Electric just reported its queue for proposed data center load has topped 8 gigawatts after signing deals with Oracle and Google.
Eight gigawatts is enormous. Graham, help me put that in perspective—what does that kind of demand actually look like for southeast Michigan?

It's enough to power hundreds of thousands of homes at peak times. This surge is driven by those two big signed agreements, and it means utilities like DTE will need major grid upgrades including new transmission lines and substations.
And residents will feel that through future electric bills, right? Who ultimately pays for all this new infrastructure?
Ratepayers do, at least in part. The story notes that decisions on where those lines and substations go will directly shape costs for southeast Michigan customers.
This isn't the first time we've seen big tech interest here. What's the history behind Michigan becoming a target for these facilities?

Data centers have been eyeing the state for a while because of available land, cooling potential in some areas, and access to the grid. But the AI boom has accelerated everything, with companies like Oracle and Google now locking in capacity.
And that acceleration is showing up in other places too. We saw Bellevue residents pushing for answers on water and power use just today.
Exactly. Neighbors there want concrete numbers on how much electricity and water a proposed facility would pull from local supplies, worrying about higher rates and strained wells.
That ties right into the bigger picture—rural towns and farmland could see real strain if these projects scale without more transparency.
Yes, and it's not just Bellevue. Across the state we're hearing similar concerns about noise, water, and power from facilities already operating or proposed.
Like the Dowagiac situation where residents are suing over constant humming that sounds like a nonstop vacuum.
The company there has already been fined and is now offering buyouts for affected homes. It shows how quality-of-life issues can escalate quickly.
And then there's the Upper Peninsula teacher who got cuffed at a meeting just for clapping against a proposal.
That incident from Monday highlights how heated these local fights have become, with residents worried about noise, rates, and water all at once.
So what happens next with this 8 gigawatt queue? Are we looking at rate cases or new transmission projects soon?

DTE will have to file for approvals on upgrades, and those will go through the public process where customers can weigh in. The deals with Oracle and Google are already signed, so the pressure is on to deliver the power.
Meanwhile DTE missed earnings targets but still landed these big contracts. How does that play into future rate decisions?
The quarterly slides show the data center deals are driving growth despite the miss. Ratepayers end up paying for the infrastructure needed to serve that new load.
That brings us to the Senate candidates who split on this exact issue over the weekend—how to regulate demand and protect ratepayers from new transmission costs.
Democratic primary contenders outlined different plans, with some wanting utilities or tech firms to cover more upgrades and others open to spreading costs across all customers.
Primary voters now have clear differences on something that will hit monthly bills. And Indiana Michigan Power made a pledge to shield residential customers from data center power line costs.
That's for parts of southwest Michigan. They're promising residents won't foot the bill, and consumer groups are watching how that holds up in actual rate cases.
Some communities are pushing back with moratoriums, like Utica extending its ban and Chippewa County weighing a freeze on new proposals.
Utica's move keeps large-scale projects out for now to protect local power and water capacity. Chippewa is studying impacts on land, power, and services before allowing more.
St. Clair County is weighing the constant humming against promised jobs, and an opinion piece there captured the tension perfectly.
Local officials everywhere are under pressure to balance tax revenue and construction work against complaints that the sound disrupts daily life.
So across the board it's about transparency and who bears the costs—whether it's bills, water, or noise.
And with the queue now over 8 gigawatts, those decisions will shape southeast Michigan for years.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
More details on where the new transmission lines will go, any rate filings from DTE, and updates from places like Bellevue and the Upper Peninsula.
And of course the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker will show the latest proposals.
Let's move to quick hits on the other stories from this week.
Starting with Bellevue—residents are demanding hard numbers on water and power use for the proposed facility.
Eaton County neighbors are concerned about higher utility rates and strained wells if the project advances without more details.
That push comes right as data centers statewide are seeking big new grid connections.
Next, DTE landed those major contracts even after missing earnings targets, with the deals expected to shape future rates and investments.
Ratepayers will ultimately pay for the infrastructure, as we discussed.
Moving to Monday, a teacher was arrested at a Michigan meeting in the Upper Peninsula just for clapping during public comments opposing a data center.
It really shows how tense these local debates have gotten over noise, power, and water.
Utica City Council voted to extend its moratorium, keeping large projects out of Macomb County for now.
That protects local capacity from sudden demand spikes and avoids immediate tax or infrastructure strain.
In St. Clair County, residents are debating the noise from new facilities against the promised jobs and tax revenue.
The Times Herald piece captured that exact tension in eastern Michigan.
Dowagiac neighbors are suing over the nonstop hum that violates noise rules, and the company is offering home buyouts after being fined.
Nearby residents could face the same issues if more projects move in without stronger sound limits.
Chippewa County leaders are considering a temporary moratorium to study impacts on land, power, and services.
That could stall or shift development pressure in the eastern Upper Peninsula.
And on Saturday the Senate candidates laid out different approaches to regulating data center electricity demand.
Some want tech firms or utilities to cover more costs, others are open to spreading them across ratepayers.
Indiana Michigan Power pledged that residential customers won't pay for new data center power lines in their service area.
Consumer groups will be watching closely as rate cases move forward.
Now for on deck—what meetings are coming up that listeners can attend?
The tracker doesn't list any major public hearings for tonight or tomorrow based on the latest agendas.
Folks should keep checking the Michigan Data Center Tracker for updates on local commission or planning meetings, especially around Bellevue and other active proposals.
Those are the best places to get the latest numbers on water, power, and potential impacts.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: DTE's 8GW Data Center Surge: Power Bills, Water Strain, and What's Next for Michigan Towns
